title: PraFFL: A Preference-Aware Scheme in Fair Federated Learning

problem.claim: Fair federated learning seeks unbiased models across groups with diverse sensitive features, while improving fairness can reduce model performance.

gap.claim: Existing preference-based approaches assume each client has one pre-defined preference and do not address practical settings in which clients have multiple preferences.

contributions.claim: PraFFL is a preference-aware fair federated learning scheme that generates preference-specific models in real time.
PraFFL adaptively adjusts the model according to each client's preferences.
The authors provide a theoretical result that PraFFL offers an optimal model for an arbitrary client preference and has linear convergence.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that PraFFL outperforms six fair federated learning algorithms in adapting to clients' different preferences.
The authors report that an implementation is available on GitHub.

narrative_sequence.summary: Fair federated learning targets unbiased models across groups with diverse sensitive features.
Fairness and model performance involve a trade-off, and existing methods represent client preferences with hyperparameters.
Existing methods do not support clients with multiple preferences.
PraFFL generates and adaptively adjusts preference-specific models in real time.
The authors report theoretical guarantees, comparative experimental gains, and a public implementation.

source_observation.claim: Clients may have multiple preferences over fairness and model performance.

interpretation.claim: Preference-aware systems may need to adapt models dynamically instead of committing each client to one fixed preference.

application.claim: In federated optimization settings with changing or multiple client objectives, consider real-time preference-specific model adaptation.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this approach applies beyond the stated fair federated learning setting.

unknowns: Datasets, evaluation metrics, and experimental settings are not specified.
The six comparison algorithms are not identified.
The assumptions and proof details behind optimality and linear convergence are not provided.
The representation and range of client preferences are not described.
